newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish PM optimistic on new IRA truce.
newsitem.headline: Irish PM optimistic on new IRA truce.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister John Bruton voiced optimism on Wednesday that Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas would call a new truce in their war against British rule of Northern Ireland.
Asked in parliament if he still believed a ceasefire was imminent, the Irish leader replied that in September he had said he had reason to believe there would be a ceasefire soon.
"That remains the case," he told opposition leader Bertie Ahern.

Bruton gave no reasons for his optimism, which contrasted sharply with assessments by British officials and Northern Irish politicians. But it chimed with a forecast by Northern Ireland police chief Sir Hugh Annesley, who said he thought the guerrillas would call a new truce to try to get their Sinn Fein political arm invited to peace talks.
The IRA ended a 17-month ceasefire in February by attacking British targets in Britain and in Germany and then struck in Northern Ireland this month with an attack on Britain's army headquarters.

Britain and Ireland, partners in an attempt to forge a lasting political settlement to 27 years of Northern Ireland conflict, say Sinn Fein cannot be invited to peace talks until there is a new IRA truce.
Sinn Fein says the talks are designed to make the IRA surrender its weapons and refuses to accept this as a precondition.

Publicly, Sinn Fein leaders have dismissed speculation of a new IRA ceasefire. They insist they should be invited to the peace talks because they are a legitimate political party which won some 15 percent of the province's votes in a poll in May to select negotiators for the peace talks.
In September, Bruton surprised his American hosts and British officials by saying there was a good chance of a new IRA ceasefire in the near future.
Speaking in New York, he said he based his optimism on the fact that the peace talks offered the first chance in almost 30 years for all parties to be involved in negotiations.
Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams quickly quashed speculation of a new IRA truce, however, and renewed his appeal for his party to be admitted to the negotiations.
The peace talks are attended by representatives of the IRA's foes, loyalist guerrillas who fought for 27 years to avenge IRA attacks and keep the province British.
Loyalist militia have abided by their own two-year old ceasefire and say they want to give the peace talks a chance.
